items.title: Human–Elephant Conflict and Habitat Fragmentation
items.text: The African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana) is the largest land animal on Earth. They are highly intelligent and live in close family groups, where knowledge is passed down from one generation to the next. In Namibia, around 24,000 elephants remained in 2021, but the species is endangered and faces growing challenges. One of the biggest threats is habitat fragmentation. Older elephants teach younger ones traditional routes to find water and food, but roads, farming, and expanding towns can disrupt these routes. As a result, elephants may travel farther and enter human settlements, where they can damage crops or property. Climate change worsens this problem by making water scarcer and increasing the likelihood of conflict with people.

items.title: Elephant Facts and Physical Traits
items.text: Adult male elephants are on average 3.3 meters tall at the shoulder, while females average about 2.7 meters. Tusks are used for digging, stripping bark, and defense during conflicts. Their ears help regulate body temperature by flapping to cool the blood. The trunk is used for breathing, smelling, touching, grasping, and producing sound. Elephants typically live 60 to 70 years, although lifespan can be affected by poaching and the availability of food and water.

items.title: Behavior, Memory, and Social Structure
items.text: Elephants live in herds with a matriarchal structure, meaning that an experienced female leads the group. Family bonds are very strong, and elephants may show distress behaviors when a family member dies. They are known for long-term memory, which helps them remember routes, resources, and social relationships.

items.title: Elephants and Biodiversity
items.text: Elephants play an important role in maintaining biodiversity. Their dung provides food for many species and helps disperse seeds across the landscape. They also dig water holes that can be used by other animals. Because they shape habitats and support other forms of life, elephants are often considered a keystone species.

items.title: Indigenous Knowledge of Elephant Behavior
items.text: Indigenous communities often have extensive knowledge of elephant behavior developed through generations of coexistence. They may predict elephant movement by observing environmental cues such as animal behavior, bird calls, or sudden quietness. In some communities, harming elephants is taboo because they are considered sacred.

items.title: Elephant Communication: Vocal Signals
items.text: Elephants use vocal signals such as low-frequency rumbles that can travel several kilometers for coordination and communication. Trumpets signal excitement or fear, while roars and grunts are associated with aggression or distress.

items.title: Elephant Communication: Non-Vocal and Seismic Signals
items.text: Elephants communicate through body language and touch, reinforcing social bonds. They can also produce ground vibrations by stomping, allowing seismic communication over long distances.
